## Difference Between Add-ons and Weakauras

An addon in TBC Anniversary is a full-featured UI modification that adds new systems or replaces parts of the game interface, such as damage meters, boss mods, action bars, or inventory management.
Addons are installed as separate folders, run continuously, and usually provide their own settings menus and long-term functionality.

A WeakAura, on the other hand, is a lightweight, highly customizable visual or audio trigger created inside the WeakAuras addon. WeakAuras are used to track very specific things like a cooldown, buff, debuff, proc, or resource, and show alerts only when certain conditions are met. In short, addons change how the game works overall, while WeakAuras give you precise, situation-based alerts on top of that.

To start using Weakauras, simply install the main addon, and then copy the import string from the aura you found interesting into the import section of the addon.

## The Burning Crusade Anniversary Best Addons FAQ

In this FAQ section, we will answer some of the most commonly asked questions about add-ons in The Burning Crusade Classic Anniversary.

### What Are Add-ons in TBC Classic Anniversary?
Add-ons improve your interface and track important info like buffs, debuffs, cooldowns, quests, and resources.

### What is the Difference between Add-ons and WeakAuras in TBC Anniversary?

Add-ons are standalone modifications that run on their own, while WeakAuras are created within the WeakAuras addon and depend on it to work.

### How Do I Install Add-ons in TBC Classic Anniversary?

You can use an addon manager like CurseForge or WowUp for easy installation and updates. You can also install manually by placing the addon folder in \_classic\_era\_/Int

results.title: Learning UI design through World of Warcraft | by Tim Froehlich | Medium
excerpts:
I discovered a fun little narrative told through the UI in the shots over time.

WoW is a game with an obscene quantity of buttons, meters, progress bars, and timers. By the end of the game, you aren’t making a lot of moment-to-moment decisions — you’re executing a sequence of skills in a rote order as quickly as possible, aiming to eliminate any downtime between the next spellcast or attack. You’re basically juggling as many timers at once as possible. So, the interface really _is_ the game. You’re staring at it constantly. And by default, it’s not that pretty.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

What drove me to start modding the UI was that my eyes were being split in 4 disparate locations of the screen — the health bars in the top left, the buff indicators in the top right, the skills at the bottom, and the actual combat taking place in the center.

## Iteration 1: Things get worse before they get better

Press enter or click to view image in full size
I found a semi-transparent HUD-like display for health and mana to overlay in the center and got a skill wheel to place closer to the center of my character. The one solid improvement was the menu bar at the top, which provided a lot of stats and quick-access buttons.

Otherwise, this is a step backwards. The curved health bars are wildly deceptive, disguising the bottom and top 20%. You practically can’t see the bars at all when you’re low on health. The skill wheel is an aesthetic dumpster fire, but did condense things down a bit for the many niche-use skills for my priest.

## Iteration 2: Ovals and squares aren’t friends

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Things got a bit easier when I switched to a rogue, which had about a third as many skills as my priest. Feeling bold and sassy, I ditched the native UI entirely and sent my skills out on a wild journey into the center of the screen, where they hover awkwardly next to the oval HUD like some kind of geometric parasite.
But still, it achieves the goal of getting the important information into the center of the screen, there’s more visual real estate to see what’s going on. The bottom of the screen is looking reasonably tidy with the chat and combat logs pushed out of the way and a little background gradient to help with legibility.

## Iteration 3: The minimap goes rogue

Press enter or click to view image in full size

I finally say goodbye to the HUD, realizing that there’s no way I can structure the interface around such a janky contraption. We’re achieving something akin to consistency with all these squares.

But then, drunk on power, I had an epiphany that I’m spending a lot of time looking at the minimap for questing purposes, so it should come hang out with the skills in the center of the screen.
But I couldn’t make it symmetrical because there’s a minimum width on the chat and combat logs, so there’s there’s gaping chasm looming wildly off-center so as to trigger any reasonable designer’s acid reflux. For some reason I also decided to swap the menu buttons and status bar between the bottom and the top, which leaves the top naked while the bottom’s all saggy and bloated with information.

## Iteration 4: Why’s the minimap a circle now?

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Apparently having learned nothing from the oval HUD, the minimap regresses into roundness. The gradient at the bottom explodes with an ugly vigor, occluding the center of the screen where there is no text to support. The menu bar now hovers ominously above this gradient wall, making the whole thing look like I’m viewing my game through some kind of picture-in-picture bullshit.

But at the very least, there’s some symmetry going on.
The skills are looking more organized, though I’m not sure what the staircase is about. I’ve managed to squeeze more skills onto the sides without adding clutter, so it’s a step up in usability.

## Iteration 5: Thank god it’s square again

Press enter or click to view image in full size

In fact, everything has become nice and rectangular! It’s looking reasonably structured, though it turns out that most of those buttons in the center are there just to fill space. It’s got problems, but we’re on an upward trend.

## Iteration 6: The prodigal’s son returns home to the goddamn corner where it belongs

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Through all these previous iterations, my buff timers have been squirreled away at the top of the screen, and as my skill rotations are getting tighter I’m finding it hard to keep track of them way off in the corner. What can I do to bring them down? Oh, right, the minimap. Thus, I solve the problem that I created for myself.
Further realizing that I don’t need buttons for cooking and disenchanting consuming the center of the screen, that whole skill section vanishes, which then eliminates any pretense of maintaining that god-forsaken gradient. I realized that I’d never need it for reading the chat logs because those become opaque on mouse hover, which clashed horridly with the gradient. Even knowing all this, I was loathe to ditch that thing. I thought it was just so _cool_ . I was _so wrong_ .

I even found some nice polished health bars which came with a fancy little sliver showing the current target’s face, which was handy for keeping track of what I was currently attacking.

Now we’re cooking with gas.

## Iteration 7: Screw minimalism, it’s time to raid

Press enter or click to view image in full size

> Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth  
> — legendary UI designer Mike Tyson
> 
>

...

A lot of people look back on their time with MMOs with mixed feelings — it can represent a lot of wasted time and energy. But for me, I learned tons of valuable lessons about UI design from modding the game, and it was a chance to hone my skills in something that would end up becoming a big part of my career a decade later. I didn’t know that’s what I was doing at the time — I was just chasing my OCD and trying to make it better.

It’s neat when doing shit for fun turns out to have practical utility.

results.title: How I Build My UI in World of Warcraft — Rambling About Games
excerpts:
basic, but the most important feature it has always had, is _mod-ability_ . Specifically, WoW has a very open-ended UI system written entirely in lua, making it very easy to mod. The modding scene has been so prevalent for so long that, customizing one's UI is almost a rite of passage at this point- it's just something that most people do when they become reasonable serious about the game.

Over the years, I've spent a _lot_ of time playing with different addons and layouts, trying to figure out exactly when and where I like my information to be displayed. I honestly attribute this practice to my first experience with UI/UX design.

Unfortunately, setting up for yet another new expansion means re-doing my UI for the umpteenth time, but I thought I would use this as an exercise, to walk you through setting up my time-tested UI; what I do, and more importantly, why.
As a note, just keep in mind that a UI in this game is a very personal thing, that's meant to serve only one's self, and achieve whatever goals the user specifically wants to accomplish. This is not inherently the same thing as creating a UI designed for this consumption of others. This is what I personally look for in my own UI.

So let's get this thing going!

View fullsize

default.jpg

Before we do anything at all, here we have the default WoW UI. It's not exactly awe-inspiring, but it's definitely way better than it once was. There's a fair amount of customization to be had here these days, and for the most part, it's pretty usable out of the box, even for end game content.

Most notable is the fact that, the unit frames (positioned at the top left in this screenshot) can be moved wherever you want. Quite handy if you don't feel like look all the way across the screen every time you want to look from your player resources to your action bar.

...

My reasoning is that, WoW is a game which is measured in hundreds of hours- if you haven't memorized what ability is on which key already, then you've got bigger problems anyways. It can definitely be helpful to be able to see these abilities to see things like cooldowns, but there are better ways to display that information that we'll be getting to in a bit.

Instead I like to break my bar up into 2 sections. On the left I have very large icons that are used for things like longer cooldowns, and anything that I may not be using moment to moment. This information is important, so positioning it on the very bottom of the screen may seem a bit far from the screen's focal point, but since we're typically talking abilities that have a cooldown of around 1-5 minutes, there's usually no need to look here more often then every 20-30 seconds.

...

well, anything. It adds a bunch of information, especially if you are hovering an NPC or player. Things like, current target, spec, health bar, and just in general pretties it up a bunch. This information isn't too useful at a glance typically, but positioning it just above recount is just a comfy home for it, and so TipTac is mostly nice just for moving the anchor point to this position.

View fullsize

final.jpg

Finally, we have the last few touches- which is the actual information we need to perform our key rotational abilities. We have [MikScrollingBattleText](https://wow.curseforge.com/projects/mik-scrolling-battle-text) displaying on the left and right edges of the game world, and information pertaining to abilities and buffs just above the player frame (usually done with a combo of extra Bartender4 bars, [TellMeWhen](https://wow.curseforge.com/projects/tellmewhen?gameCategorySlug=addons&projectID=8025) , and [WeakAuras2](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/WeakAuras-2?

...

If I'm not careful, this particular part of the UI can tend to encroach on the game world a little bit, but this is also the most important part of the entire UI, and this is where I intend to be looking at basically all times. This is the crux of it all, and basically everything is designed around how far I have to look from that point if I'm looking for a specific piece of information.

View fullsize

final_marked.jpg

And that's basically it. Obviously there's more stuff that goes into a UI, things like cast bars (I use [Quartz](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/quartz) for these), raid frames (which I use the stock blizzard ones), [DeadlyBossMods](https://wow.curseforge.com/projects/deadly-boss-mods) for raid encounters, and so on. These things always tend to occupy the outside edges of the screen, but you can see what I mean by that down below. For reference, here is the "final" UI with the focal points drawn on it again, now that everything is in place.
